For some people, university means a new city, new friends, and being able to make decisions without checking with family first. That can be incredible. It can also create pressure to prove that you're living the kind of college experience you see in movies or online. My goal isn't to prescribe one social life. It's to ask how we build a life that's exciting and genuinely ours, while taking health, safety, and friendships seriously.
I want to give you a tiny experiment. Think of the last message you almost sent while annoyed. How different might the conversation have been if you had waited five seconds?

People sometimes think the goal of prevention is to make life smaller: fewer invitations, fewer experiences, less fun. I see it differently. The point is to expand choice. It's to make space for students who have different values, cultures, ambitions, and comfort levels. When everyone feels forced into a single version of being young, the group loses something. When people can participate without pretending to be someone else, there is more room for genuine connection. Keep that idea in the background as we explore today's question.

A pause is not a guarantee of a good decision, but it can create space between an impulse and an action. Our brains continuously balance emotion, attention, learned habits, and goals. You can feel excluded and still choose a response that protects your future.

On a campus, a single weekend can seem strangely symbolic. People talk about who went where, who knows whom, and which event everybody supposedly attended. Yet the best part of university is that there are hundreds of possible communities. You can find people through research, sports, music, service, entrepreneurship, and quiet conversations over food. If one social setting pressures you to act against your values, it doesn't mean you're failing at campus life. It might mean you haven't yet discovered the other spaces where you fit more naturally. Freedom is not the absence of boundaries; it's the ability to choose them.

Good intentions are a start, not a method.
I want to give you a tiny experiment. Think of the last message you almost sent while annoyed. How different might the conversation have been if you had waited five seconds?

Before we get into the main idea, I want to make one distinction. Information is not the same as judgment. I'm not here to inspect anybody's private decisions or ask who has and hasn't done something. I'm here because we make better choices when we have accurate information, supportive people, and a chance to think before the pressure arrives. If there is a detail you disagree with, question it. If there is a concept you recognize from your own life, hold on to it. This should be useful long after the chairs in this room have been put away.

When you're a leader, the challenge is to turn an individual message into an experience people can actually use. A student can hear an inspiring talk and still face the same peer pressure that evening. So ask what changes around them afterward. Do they have language for setting boundaries? Are there social alternatives? Do they know where to get help? Is a trusted adult available? Can quieter students participate without disclosing private experiences? These questions make prevention more practical and help us avoid thinking that a dramatic presentation is the same thing as lasting impact.

Imagine receiving an invitation with the message, 'Everybody's going, don't be lame.' Your instinct may be to say yes before finding out where the event is or how you will get home. Here's a second way of testing the idea. Imagine you disagree with part of what I've said. What would a thoughtful question sound like? I want to resist two extreme stories. One says young people are incapable of good judgment and need only orders. The other says that because risk is part of life, understanding it doesn't matter. Neither helps us. Good education respects people's agency while giving them tools and realistic information.

Practice the sequence: notice, name, choose. Notice the rush of urgency. Name what you are feeling: anxious, curious, frustrated, eager to impress. Then choose one action that reflects what matters to you. It might be asking a question, saying no, calling a friend, or simply waiting until you have more information. Start with low-stakes situations, like responding to a group chat. Skills are easier to use under pressure when they are familiar beforehand.

For a moment, picture the last event or workshop you helped organize. Now think of the student who sat at the back and said nothing. Did the design of the session help that person feel safe and included, or did all the attention go to whoever was already confident? This isn't a criticism. It's a design test. We should measure success partly by what becomes possible for the person who didn't arrive with social capital. That means asking for feedback, working within safeguarding requirements, and making sure our actions match the respectful language we use on stage.
Five seconds will not solve every problem. But sometimes a few seconds are enough to remember that you are the person who gets to decide what happens next.

I'll leave you with a specific assignment. Choose one part of your school or group culture you can improve within thirty days. Talk to the people affected, involve the appropriate adults or professionals, and define a realistic way to learn whether the change helped. Document the process so another group can build on it. SoberGenZ should stand for responsible action, not just confident words. Thank you for the work you do for young people.

title: Prevention Without Shame | Younger secondary students
primary_topic: Prevention Without Shame

sections.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm speaking with you today through SoberGenZ. Some of you may have heard older students talk about parties or drinking and wondered what those conversations have to do with you. You do not need to have any experience with alcohol to be part of this discussion. We are here to build a skill before you are expected to use it: thinking for yourself in a room full of other people. There will be no requests to share personal stories in front of the class. You can take part by thinking, listening, or asking a general question. The goal is to leave with language you can actually use outside this room.
A prevention message can be scientifically accurate and still fail if the people hearing it feel judged, embarrassed, or dismissed.

Before we get into the main idea, I want to make one distinction. Information is not the same as judgment. I'm not here to inspect anybody's private decisions or ask who has and hasn't done something. I'm here because we make better choices when we have accurate information, supportive people, and a chance to think before the pressure arrives. If there is a detail you disagree with, question it. If there is a concept you recognize from your own life, hold on to it. This should be useful long after the chairs in this room have been put away.

People who have questions or difficult experiences involving alcohol need room to ask for help. If every conversation divides the world into good people and bad people, those who most need reliable information may be the least likely to speak. We can state clearly that alcohol carries risks, that young people deserve protection from those risks, and that safer choices matter. We can do all of that without humiliating anybody. Substance-related problems can be complex and may require professional assessment or treatment. A school session should never pretend that a few motivational lines replace that support. What we can do is increase understanding, reduce fear of asking for assistance, and make accurate resources easier to find.

At your age, many important social moments happen in places adults might consider ordinary: a lunch table, a birthday, a class group chat, the corridor after school. Someone makes a joke, somebody tries to impress the group, and a small decision suddenly feels huge. That's why I don't want you to hear today's ideas as a lecture about a distant future. Think about the moments you already face: being dared to say something unkind, being pushed to join an activity, or staying quiet when a friend needs support. The same decision skills apply. You can practice them now with situations that are safer and more familiar.

Imagine two presentations. In the first, a speaker asks students to raise their hands and publicly admit experiences they may not want to share. In the second, students can ask anonymous questions, hear clear information, and learn where to seek confidential help. Which room is more likely to produce an honest conversation? The second room does not require the presenter to approve of risky behavior. It requires the presenter to respect the audience's dignity. Trust is not a bonus in prevention work. It is part of how the work becomes possible.
If this sounds abstract, put the idea into a school lunch break. The decisions in front of you may seem smaller, but the habit of noticing pressure begins there.

Here's a second way of testing the idea. Imagine you disagree with part of what I've said. What would a thoughtful question sound like? It might be about how people behave in different cultures, what the science really supports, or why some choices seem harder than others. Asking those questions is a sign of engagement, not disrespect. We want people to develop judgment, and judgment improves through careful questioning. A prevention movement that cannot tolerate honest questions won't be a very useful one.

I want to resist two extreme stories. One says young people are incapable of good judgment and need only orders. The other says that because risk is part of life, understanding it doesn't matter. Neither helps us. Good education respects people's agency while giving them tools and realistic information.

When you speak about someone facing a challenge, describe the behavior or situation rather than treating it as the person's entire identity. Do not demand personal disclosures in group settings. Provide pathways to qualified support, and follow local safeguarding requirements when working with minors. If a friend tells you something worrying, listen seriously, avoid promising secrecy you cannot safely keep, and encourage help from appropriate adults or professionals. Our aim is to make the next safe step easier, not the person smaller.

Let me ask you a question, and you can answer silently. Think of a person your age you respect. What makes them impressive? Is it that they copy the loudest person in the room, or that they seem comfortable doing what they believe is right? Take ten seconds to picture one specific action you admired. Maybe they included a new student, stood up for a friend, or admitted a mistake. That action is what courage looks like in everyday life. Whatever your answer, keep it in mind when we talk about making choices.
The strongest prevention message is both clear and humane. We can protect young people without making them afraid to tell us the truth.

Before I finish, pick one sentence you can take from this room and use this week. It might be 'I'm good, thanks,' 'What do you want to do instead?' or 'Are you okay?' You don't need to make a dramatic announcement. Try it once where it matters. Thank you for listening, and remember that a thoughtful choice is something you can practice long before a difficult situation arrives.

sections.text: Hi, everyone. I'm here with SoberGenZ, and I want this to feel more like a real conversation than another adult-style warning speech. You already make complicated choices. You manage coursework, friendships, family expectations, relationships, and a social world that can move very quickly. The point today is not to assume you're reckless, and it certainly isn't to pretend that every person in this room has the same experience. It's to look at what actually shapes our decisions and how we keep control over them. You won't have to disclose anything personal. The questions I ask are for reflection, not for a public confession.
A prevention message can be scientifically accurate and still fail if the people hearing it feel judged, embarrassed, or dismissed.

Part of the reason I care about this work is that we often underestimate young people. We give them slogans when they deserve explanations. We give them lists of rules when they also need social skills and trustworthy relationships. So today, I want to connect the science to everyday behavior. You do not have to memorize terminology. You do have to get curious about why a choice that seems simple from a distance can feel complicated when you are standing in the middle of it.

People who have questions or difficult experiences involving alcohol need room to ask for help. If every conversation divides the world into good people and bad people, those who most need reliable information may be the least likely to speak. We can state clearly that alcohol carries risks, that young people deserve protection from those risks, and that safer choices matter. We can do all of that without humiliating anybody. Substance-related problems can be complex and may require professional assessment or treatment. A school session should never pretend that a few motivational lines replace that support. What we can do is increase understanding, reduce fear of asking for assistance, and make accurate resources easier to find.

There's a particular kind of pressure that comes with being old enough to want independence and young enough for other people to constantly define what independence should look like. One group might expect you to be adventurous. Another might expect you to be perfect. Neither group gets to write the entire definition of maturity for you. What matters is whether you can consider a consequence, set a boundary, and still build a full social life. The choices we discuss today are not only about alcohol. They touch confidence, loyalty, ambition, and what kind of friends we want to be.

Imagine two presentations. In the first, a speaker asks students to raise their hands and publicly admit experiences they may not want to share. In the second, students can ask anonymous questions, hear clear information, and learn where to seek confidential help. Which room is more likely to produce an honest conversation? The second room does not require the presenter to approve of risky behavior. It requires the presenter to respect the audience's dignity. Trust is not a bonus in prevention work. It is part of how the work becomes possible.
Imagine a group chat where the first response seems to decide everybody else's plans. One question from you can reveal the options nobody has mentioned.

There is another person I want you to consider: the student who is listening to this and thinks, 'That's easy for someone else to say.' They might have a difficult home life, a complicated social circle, or fewer options for getting home safely. If we want our advice to be genuinely useful, we have to notice those constraints. We can encourage personal responsibility while recognizing that not everybody starts from the same circumstances. A strong community makes safer choices easier and provides support when someone needs more than a motivational sentence.

As we discuss this, notice the gap between what sounds impressive and what works. A dramatic promise is easy to make. A simple plan, a respectful friend, or an accessible support system might look less exciting, but those are often what people can use when a real decision arrives.

When you speak about someone facing a challenge, describe the behavior or situation rather than treating it as the person's entire identity. Do not demand personal disclosures in group settings. Provide pathways to qualified support, and follow local safeguarding requirements when working with minors. If a friend tells you something worrying, listen seriously, avoid promising secrecy you cannot safely keep, and encourage help from appropriate adults or professionals. Our aim is to make the next safe step easier, not the person smaller.

I want you to picture a Friday evening six months from now. You have an invitation, you're tired, and you have a genuine reason to feel torn. What information would help you decide well? Think about who will be there, whether you feel comfortable, what you need the next day, and how you would leave if your plans changed. Now ask yourself whether you usually consider those things before or after saying yes. There's no perfect answer, but there is a skill in making a decision before social momentum makes it for you.
The strongest prevention message is both clear and humane. We can protect young people without making them afraid to tell us the truth.

I'll end with one challenge: choose one thing you currently do because it's expected, and ask yourself whether you'd choose it without an audience. You don't have to change anything just to prove a point. I just want the answer to be yours. If you remember one idea from SoberGenZ, let it be that you can have meaningful friendships, spontaneity, and excitement without surrendering the right to decide what you're comfortable with. Thank you.

What matters is whether you can consider a consequence, set a boundary, and still build a full social life. The choices we discuss today are not only about alcohol. They touch confidence, loyalty, ambition, and what kind of friends we want to be.

It is part of how the work becomes possible.

Imagine a group chat where the first response seems to decide everybody else's plans. One question from you can reveal the options nobody has mentioned.

We can encourage personal responsibility while recognizing that not everybody starts from the same circumstances. title: Prevention Without Shame | University students and new adults
primary_topic: Prevention Without Shame

sections.text: Thanks for having me. I'm speaking through SoberGenZ, and I want to start with the freedom that comes when you leave a familiar environment. For some people, university means a new city, new friends, and being able to make decisions without checking with family first. That can be incredible. It can also create pressure to prove that you're living the kind of college experience you see in movies or online. My goal isn't to prescribe one social life. It's to ask how we build a life that's exciting and genuinely ours, while taking health, safety, and friendships seriously.
A prevention message can be scientifically accurate and still fail if the people hearing it feel judged, embarrassed, or dismissed.

I also want to make clear what this session cannot do. One talk does not fix a stressful environment, replace medical advice, or solve every challenge a student might face. But a talk can change the next conversation. It can give someone language for a boundary, remind a group that they have alternatives, or encourage a person to seek proper support. Those are real, practical goals. We don't need to exaggerate our power to make the effort worthwhile.

People who have questions or difficult experiences involving alcohol need room to ask for help. If every conversation divides the world into good people and bad people, those who most need reliable information may be the least likely to speak. We can state clearly that alcohol carries risks, that young people deserve protection from those risks, and that safer choices matter. We can do all of that without humiliating anybody. Substance-related problems can be complex and may require professional assessment or treatment. A school session should never pretend that a few motivational lines replace that support. What we can do is increase understanding, reduce fear of asking for assistance, and make accurate resources easier to find.

On a campus, a single weekend can seem strangely symbolic. People talk about who went where, who knows whom, and which event everybody supposedly attended. Yet the best part of university is that there are hundreds of possible communities. You can find people through research, sports, music, service, entrepreneurship, and quiet conversations over food. If one social setting pressures you to act against your values, it doesn't mean you're failing at campus life. It might mean you haven't yet discovered the other spaces where you fit more naturally. Freedom is not the absence of boundaries; it's the ability to choose them.

Imagine two presentations. In the first, a speaker asks students to raise their hands and publicly admit experiences they may not want to share. In the second, students can ask anonymous questions, hear clear information, and learn where to seek confidential help. Which room is more likely to produce an honest conversation? The second room does not require the presenter to approve of risky behavior. It requires the presenter to respect the audience's dignity. Trust is not a bonus in prevention work. It is part of how the work becomes possible.
There will always be one more invitation, one more event, and one more opportunity to miss out on something. Choose with the bigger picture in mind.

Let's turn this around for a moment. Instead of asking how you personally should act, ask what you could change for the next person in your situation. Could you make it easier for a friend to decline something? Could you be the person who invites someone new? Could you check in without judgment, or organize an activity where participation doesn't depend on drinking? Sometimes the most sustainable form of self-confidence is not simply resisting pressure but reducing it for everybody around you.

This may sound like a small distinction, but small distinctions are exactly what shape behavior in real settings. When we remove the drama, we are left with a series of decisions that can be prepared for, discussed, and improved. None of us will get every decision right. That should make us more interested in learning, not less.

When you speak about someone facing a challenge, describe the behavior or situation rather than treating it as the person's entire identity. Do not demand personal disclosures in group settings. Provide pathways to qualified support, and follow local safeguarding requirements when working with minors. If a friend tells you something worrying, listen seriously, avoid promising secrecy you cannot safely keep, and encourage help from appropriate adults or professionals. Our aim is to make the next safe step easier, not the person smaller.

Here's a short thought experiment. Imagine the next ten weekends on campus. You cannot say yes to every invitation and still have time to sleep, study, train, work, and stay close to the people you care about. So you have to choose. What kind of memories would you actually like to have at the end of the term? A few spectacular events? A solid group of friends? Progress on a project? Ideally some mix. The point is that saying no to one thing can be saying yes to something else that matters more. That's what makes intentionality useful, not restrictive.
The strongest prevention message is both clear and humane. We can protect young people without making them afraid to tell us the truth.

As you leave, I hope you'll do more than think about what to avoid. Think about what you want to create. Host something inclusive, make room for a friend who doesn't drink, check that people can get home safely, or build a group around something you love. You have an unusual amount of influence over the culture of the communities you're joining. Use that influence thoughtfully. Thanks for being here.

title: Prevention Without Shame | Student leaders, educators, and youth ambassadors
primary_topic: Prevention Without Shame
audience: Student leaders, educators, and youth ambassadors

sections.text: Hello, and thank you for giving your time to this SoberGenZ session. Some of you help run school clubs, teach, lead student groups, or organize events. That means the decisions you make can affect more than one person. I want to approach this as a working session about what effective prevention sounds like and how we can build environments that support good choices. We should be willing to talk about alcohol-related harms clearly. We should also be willing to listen, adapt, admit uncertainty, and protect the dignity of the students we work with. Good intentions are a start, not a method.
A prevention message can be scientifically accurate and still fail if the people hearing it feel judged, embarrassed, or dismissed.

People sometimes think the goal of prevention is to make life smaller: fewer invitations, fewer experiences, less fun. I see it differently. The point is to expand choice. It's to make space for students who have different values, cultures, ambitions, and comfort levels. When everyone feels forced into a single version of being young, the group loses something. When people can participate without pretending to be someone else, there is more room for genuine connection. Keep that idea in the background as we explore today's question.

People who have questions or difficult experiences involving alcohol need room to ask for help. If every conversation divides the world into good people and bad people, those who most need reliable information may be the least likely to speak. We can state clearly that alcohol carries risks, that young people deserve protection from those risks, and that safer choices matter. We can do all of that without humiliating anybody. Substance-related problems can be complex and may require professional assessment or treatment. A school session should never pretend that a few motivational lines replace that support. What we can do is increase understanding, reduce fear of asking for assistance, and make accurate resources easier to find.

When you're a leader, the challenge is to turn an individual message into an experience people can actually use. A student can hear an inspiring talk and still face the same peer pressure that evening. So ask what changes around them afterward. Do they have language for setting boundaries? Are there social alternatives? Do they know where to get help? Is a trusted adult available? Can quieter students participate without disclosing private experiences? These questions make prevention more practical and help us avoid thinking that a dramatic presentation is the same thing as lasting impact.

Imagine two presentations. In the first, a speaker asks students to raise their hands and publicly admit experiences they may not want to share. In the second, students can ask anonymous questions, hear clear information, and learn where to seek confidential help. Which room is more likely to produce an honest conversation? The second room does not require the presenter to approve of risky behavior. It requires the presenter to respect the audience's dignity. Trust is not a bonus in prevention work. It is part of how the work becomes possible.
A successful ambassador is not the person with the most dramatic speech. It is the person whose audience leaves with something usable.

I want you to take five quiet seconds here. Think about how you would explain this idea to a friend who wasn't in the room. Try to do it without using a big scientific word or repeating my phrasing. What would you say in ordinary language? If an idea is going to affect your decisions, it needs to survive outside a classroom. That's the standard I want us to use. If your explanation feels awkward at first, that's completely normal. Practice helps us turn information into something available when it matters.

The reason this topic matters is that it lives at the intersection of science and culture. You can understand a health risk perfectly and still struggle when the surrounding environment rewards a different choice. That's why I keep coming back to the people, routines, and spaces around us, not just individual willpower.

When you speak about someone facing a challenge, describe the behavior or situation rather than treating it as the person's entire identity. Do not demand personal disclosures in group settings. Provide pathways to qualified support, and follow local safeguarding requirements when working with minors. If a friend tells you something worrying, listen seriously, avoid promising secrecy you cannot safely keep, and encourage help from appropriate adults or professionals. Our aim is to make the next safe step easier, not the person smaller.

For a moment, picture the last event or workshop you helped organize. Now think of the student who sat at the back and said nothing. Did the design of the session help that person feel safe and included, or did all the attention go to whoever was already confident? This isn't a criticism. It's a design test. We should measure success partly by what becomes possible for the person who didn't arrive with social capital. That means asking for feedback, working within safeguarding requirements, and making sure our actions match the respectful language we use on stage.
The strongest prevention message is both clear and humane. We can protect young people without making them afraid to tell us the truth.

I'll leave you with a specific assignment. Choose one part of your school or group culture you can improve within thirty days. Talk to the people affected, involve the appropriate adults or professionals, and define a realistic way to learn whether the change helped. Document the process so another group can build on it. SoberGenZ should stand for responsible action, not just confident words. Thank you for the work you do for young people.

title: What Would Future You Thank You For? | Younger secondary students
primary_topic: What Would Future You Thank You For?

sections.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm speaking with you today through SoberGenZ. Some of you may have heard older students talk about parties or drinking and wondered what those conversations have to do with you. You do not need to have any experience with alcohol to be part of this discussion. We are here to build a skill before you are expected to use it: thinking for yourself in a room full of other people. There will be no requests to share personal stories in front of the class. You can take part by thinking, listening, or asking a general question. The goal is to leave with language you can actually use outside this room.
Let's do something unusual. For a moment, imagine you are writing a thank-you letter to yourself, but the person receiving it is ten years older.

People sometimes think the goal of prevention is to make life smaller: fewer invitations, fewer experiences, less fun. I see it differently. The point is to expand choice. It's to make space for students who have different values, cultures, ambitions, and comfort levels. When everyone feels forced into a single version of being young, the group loses something. When people can participate without pretending to be someone else, there is more room for genuine connection. Keep that idea in the background as we explore today's question.

We often talk about long-term goals as if they are separate from daily life. We want to be healthy, respected, capable, and surrounded by people we trust, yet we make choices when we are tired or distracted without connecting them to those goals. The future can feel abstract. One way to make it more concrete is to think about what an older version of yourself would value: attention, friendships, good memories, skills, opportunities, and the ability to recover when life gets hard. Avoiding unnecessary alcohol-related harms can support that future, but so can sleep, learning, movement, and asking for help. It is not about demanding perfection. It is about noticing that small choices form the environment in which big possibilities grow.

At your age, many important social moments happen in places adults might consider ordinary: a lunch table, a birthday, a class group chat, the corridor after school. Someone makes a joke, somebody tries to impress the group, and a small decision suddenly feels huge. That's why I don't want you to hear today's ideas as a lecture about a distant future. Think about the moments you already face: being dared to say something unkind, being pushed to join an activity, or staying quiet when a friend needs support. The same decision skills apply. You can practice them now with situations that are safer and more familiar.

Imagine you are deciding whether to stay in a setting where you are uncomfortable because you don't want to disappoint a group. Future-you cannot send you a message from ten years ahead. But you can borrow their perspective. Would they be impressed that you ignored your own discomfort for another hour? Or would they be grateful that you went home safely, kept a friendship with somebody respectful, and woke up able to do the things that matter to you? The answer might differ by situation. The useful skill is remembering that the person who handles the consequences is still you.
Think about a group project where one person decides for everyone. The skill we're discussing also helps you make room for quieter classmates.

I want you to take five quiet seconds here. Think about how you would explain this idea to a friend who wasn't in the room. Try to do it without using a big scientific word or repeating my phrasing. What would you say in ordinary language? If an idea is going to affect your decisions, it needs to survive outside a classroom. That's the standard I want us to use. If your explanation feels awkward at first, that's completely normal. Practice helps us turn information into something available when it matters.

The reason this topic matters is that it lives at the intersection of science and culture. You can understand a health risk perfectly and still struggle when the surrounding environment rewards a different choice. That's why I keep coming back to the people, routines, and spaces around us, not just individual willpower.

Write a sentence beginning, 'In ten years, I hope I am someone who...' Finish it with a quality rather than a status symbol: someone who keeps promises, knows when to ask for help, protects friends, or follows through on meaningful work. Then choose a decision you can make this week that supports that quality. The action should be small enough to be believable. You are practicing a direction, not signing a contract for a flawless future.

Let me ask you a question, and you can answer silently. Think of a person your age you respect. What makes them impressive? Is it that they copy the loudest person in the room, or that they seem comfortable doing what they believe is right? Take ten seconds to picture one specific action you admired. Maybe they included a new student, stood up for a friend, or admitted a mistake. That action is what courage looks like in everyday life. Whatever your answer, keep it in mind when we talk about making choices.
Your future is not predetermined, and circumstances matter. But you have influence over it. Use that influence to build a life that a younger version of you would feel safe growing into.

Before I finish, pick one sentence you can take from this room and use this week. It might be 'I'm good, thanks,' 'What do you want to do instead?' or 'Are you okay?' You don't need to make a dramatic announcement. Try it once where it matters. Thank you for listening, and remember that a thoughtful choice is something you can practice long before a difficult situation arrives.

title: What Would Future You Thank You For? | Older secondary students
primary_topic: What Would Future You Thank You For?

sections.text: Hi, everyone. I'm here with SoberGenZ, and I want this to feel more like a real conversation than another adult-style warning speech. You already make complicated choices. You manage coursework, friendships, family expectations, relationships, and a social world that can move very quickly. The point today is not to assume you're reckless, and it certainly isn't to pretend that every person in this room has the same experience. It's to look at what actually shapes our decisions and how we keep control over them. You won't have to disclose anything personal. The questions I ask are for reflection, not for a public confession.
Let's do something unusual. For a moment, imagine you are writing a thank-you letter to yourself, but the person receiving it is ten years older.

Before we get into the main idea, I want to make one distinction. Information is not the same as judgment. I'm not here to inspect anybody's private decisions or ask who has and hasn't done something. I'm here because we make better choices when we have accurate information, supportive people, and a chance to think before the pressure arrives. If there is a detail you disagree with, question it. If there is a concept you recognize from your own life, hold on to it. This should be useful long after the chairs in this room have been put away.

We often talk about long-term goals as if they are separate from daily life. We want to be healthy, respected, capable, and surrounded by people we trust, yet we make choices when we are tired or distracted without connecting them to those goals. The future can feel abstract. One way to make it more concrete is to think about what an older version of yourself would value: attention, friendships, good memories, skills, opportunities, and the ability to recover when life gets hard. Avoiding unnecessary alcohol-related harms can support that future, but so can sleep, learning, movement, and asking for help. It is not about demanding perfection. It is about noticing that small choices form the environment in which big possibilities grow.

There's a particular kind of pressure that comes with being old enough to want independence and young enough for other people to constantly define what independence should look like. One group might expect you to be adventurous. Another might expect you to be perfect. Neither group gets to write the entire definition of maturity for you. What matters is whether you can consider a consequence, set a boundary, and still build a full social life. The choices we discuss today are not only about alcohol. They touch confidence, loyalty, ambition, and what kind of friends we want to be.

Imagine you are deciding whether to stay in a setting where you are uncomfortable because you don't want to disappoint a group. Future-you cannot send you a message from ten years ahead. But you can borrow their perspective. Would they be impressed that you ignored your own discomfort for another hour? Or would they be grateful that you went home safely, kept a friendship with somebody respectful, and woke up able to do the things that matter to you? The answer might differ by situation. The useful skill is remembering that the person who handles the consequences is still you.
For anyone balancing coursework and a social calendar, remember that the person who wakes up tomorrow gets a vote in tonight's plans too.

Here's a second way of testing the idea. Imagine you disagree with part of what I've said. What would a thoughtful question sound like? It might be about how people behave in different cultures, what the science really supports, or why some choices seem harder than others. Asking those questions is a sign of engagement, not disrespect. We want people to develop judgment, and judgment improves through careful questioning. A prevention movement that cannot tolerate honest questions won't be a very useful one.

I want to resist two extreme stories. One says young people are incapable of good judgment and need only orders. The other says that because risk is part of life, understanding it doesn't matter. Neither helps us. Good education respects people's agency while giving them tools and realistic information.

Write a sentence beginning, 'In ten years, I hope I am someone who...' Finish it with a quality rather than a status symbol: someone who keeps promises, knows when to ask for help, protects friends, or follows through on meaningful work. Then choose a decision you can make this week that supports that quality. The action should be small enough to be believable. You are practicing a direction, not signing a contract for a flawless future.

I want you to picture a Friday evening six months from now. You have an invitation, you're tired, and you have a genuine reason to feel torn. What information would help you decide well? Think about who will be there, whether you feel comfortable, what you need the next day, and how you would leave if your plans changed. Now ask yourself whether you usually consider those things before or after saying yes. There's no perfect answer, but there is a skill in making a decision before social momentum makes it for you.
Your future is not predetermined, and circumstances matter. But you have influence over it. Use that influence to build a life that a younger version of you would feel safe growing into.

I'll end with one challenge: choose one thing you currently do because it's expected, and ask yourself whether you'd choose it without an audience. You don't have to change anything just to prove a point. I just want the answer to be yours. If you remember one idea from SoberGenZ, let it be that you can have meaningful friendships, spontaneity, and excitement without surrendering the right to decide what you're comfortable with. Thank you.

title: What Would Future You Thank You For? | University students and new adults
primary_topic: What Would Future You Thank You For?

sections.text: Thanks for having me. I'm speaking through SoberGenZ, and I want to start with the freedom that comes when you leave a familiar environment. For some people, university means a new city, new friends, and being able to make decisions without checking with family first. That can be incredible. It can also create pressure to prove that you're living the kind of college experience you see in movies or online. My goal isn't to prescribe one social life. It's to ask how we build a life that's exciting and genuinely ours, while taking health, safety, and friendships seriously.
Let's do something unusual. For a moment, imagine you are writing a thank-you letter to yourself, but the person receiving it is ten years older.

Part of the reason I care about this work is that we often underestimate young people. We give them slogans when they deserve explanations. We give them lists of rules when they also need social skills and trustworthy relationships. So today, I want to connect the science to everyday behavior. You do not have to memorize terminology. You do have to get curious about why a choice that seems simple from a distance can feel complicated when you are standing in the middle of it.

We often talk about long-term goals as if they are separate from daily life. We want to be healthy, respected, capable, and surrounded by people we trust, yet we make choices when we are tired or distracted without connecting them to those goals. The future can feel abstract. One way to make it more concrete is to think about what an older version of yourself would value: attention, friendships, good memories, skills, opportunities, and the ability to recover when life gets hard. Avoiding unnecessary alcohol-related harms can support that future, but so can sleep, learning, movement, and asking for help. It is not about demanding perfection. It is about noticing that small choices form the environment in which big possibilities grow.

On a campus, a single weekend can seem strangely symbolic. People talk about who went where, who knows whom, and which event everybody supposedly attended. Yet the best part of university is that there are hundreds of possible communities. You can find people through research, sports, music, service, entrepreneurship, and quiet conversations over food. If one social setting pressures you to act against your values, it doesn't mean you're failing at campus life. It might mean you haven't yet discovered the other spaces where you fit more naturally. Freedom is not the absence of boundaries; it's the ability to choose them.

Imagine you are deciding whether to stay in a setting where you are uncomfortable because you don't want to disappoint a group. Future-you cannot send you a message from ten years ahead. But you can borrow their perspective. Would they be impressed that you ignored your own discomfort for another hour? Or would they be grateful that you went home safely, kept a friendship with somebody respectful, and woke up able to do the things that matter to you? The answer might differ by situation. The useful skill is remembering that the person who handles the consequences is still you.
When you arrive somewhere new, the quiet decision to find people who respect you can matter more than being seen in the loudest room.

There is another person I want you to consider: the student who is listening to this and thinks, 'That's easy for someone else to say.' They might have a difficult home life, a complicated social circle, or fewer options for getting home safely. If we want our advice to be genuinely useful, we have to notice those constraints. We can encourage personal responsibility while recognizing that not everybody starts from the same circumstances. A strong community makes safer choices easier and provides support when someone needs more than a motivational sentence.

As we discuss this, notice the gap between what sounds impressive and what works. A dramatic promise is easy to make. A simple plan, a respectful friend, or an accessible support system might look less exciting, but those are often what people can use when a real decision arrives.

Write a sentence beginning, 'In ten years, I hope I am someone who...' Finish it with a quality rather than a status symbol: someone who keeps promises, knows when to ask for help, protects friends, or follows through on meaningful work. Then choose a decision you can make this week that supports that quality. The action should be small enough to be believable. You are practicing a direction, not signing a contract for a flawless future.

Here's a short thought experiment. Imagine the next ten weekends on campus. You cannot say yes to every invitation and still have time to sleep, study, train, work, and stay close to the people you care about. So you have to choose. What kind of memories would you actually like to have at the end of the term? A few spectacular events? A solid group of friends? Progress on a project? Ideally some mix. The point is that saying no to one thing can be saying yes to something else that matters more. That's what makes intentionality useful, not restrictive.
Your future is not predetermined, and circumstances matter. But you have influence over it. Use that influence to build a life that a younger version of you would feel safe growing into.

As you leave, I hope you'll do more than think about what to avoid. Think about what you want to create. Host something inclusive, make room for a friend who doesn't drink, check that people can get home safely, or build a group around something you love. You have an unusual amount of influence over the culture of the communities you're joining. Use that influence thoughtfully. Thanks for being here.

title: What Would Future You Thank You For? | Student leaders, educators, and youth ambassadors
primary_topic: What Would Future You Thank You For?
audience: Student leaders, educators, and youth ambassadors

sections.text: Hello, and thank you for giving your time to this SoberGenZ session. Some of you help run school clubs, teach, lead student groups, or organize events. That means the decisions you make can affect more than one person. I want to approach this as a working session about what effective prevention sounds like and how we can build environments that support good choices. We should be willing to talk about alcohol-related harms clearly. We should also be willing to listen, adapt, admit uncertainty, and protect the dignity of the students we work with. Good intentions are a start, not a method.
Let's do something unusual. For a moment, imagine you are writing a thank-you letter to yourself, but the person receiving it is ten years older.

I also want to make clear what this session cannot do. One talk does not fix a stressful environment, replace medical advice, or solve every challenge a student might face. But a talk can change the next conversation. It can give someone language for a boundary, remind a group that they have alternatives, or encourage a person to seek proper support. Those are real, practical goals. We don't need to exaggerate our power to make the effort worthwhile.

We often talk about long-term goals as if they are separate from daily life. We want to be healthy, respected, capable, and surrounded by people we trust, yet we make choices when we are tired or distracted without connecting them to those goals. The future can feel abstract. One way to make it more concrete is to think about what an older version of yourself would value: attention, friendships, good memories, skills, opportunities, and the ability to recover when life gets hard. Avoiding unnecessary alcohol-related harms can support that future, but so can sleep, learning, movement, and asking for help. It is not about demanding perfection. It is about noticing that small choices form the environment in which big possibilities grow.

When you're a leader, the challenge is to turn an individual message into an experience people can actually use. A student can hear an inspiring talk and still face the same peer pressure that evening. So ask what changes around them afterward. Do they have language for setting boundaries? Are there social alternatives? Do they know where to get help? Is a trusted adult available? Can quieter students participate without disclosing private experiences? These questions make prevention more practical and help us avoid thinking that a dramatic presentation is the same thing as lasting impact.

Imagine you are deciding whether to stay in a setting where you are uncomfortable because you don't want to disappoint a group. Future-you cannot send you a message from ten years ahead. But you can borrow their perspective. Would they be impressed that you ignored your own discomfort for another hour? Or would they be grateful that you went home safely, kept a friendship with somebody respectful, and woke up able to do the things that matter to you? The answer might differ by situation. The useful skill is remembering that the person who handles the consequences is still you.
Think about a workshop where the audience understands the facts but lacks a way to use them. Our job is to close that gap through practice and support.

Let's turn this around for a moment. Instead of asking how you personally should act, ask what you could change for the next person in your situation. Could you make it easier for a friend to decline something? Could you be the person who invites someone new? Could you check in without judgment, or organize an activity where participation doesn't depend on drinking? Sometimes the most sustainable form of self-confidence is not simply resisting pressure but reducing it for everybody around you.

This may sound like a small distinction, but small distinctions are exactly what shape behavior in real settings. When we remove the drama, we are left with a series of decisions that can be prepared for, discussed, and improved. None of us will get every decision right. That should make us more interested in learning, not less.

Write a sentence beginning, 'In ten years, I hope I am someone who...' Finish it with a quality rather than a status symbol: someone who keeps promises, knows when to ask for help, protects friends, or follows through on meaningful work. Then choose a decision you can make this week that supports that quality. The action should be small enough to be believable. You are practicing a direction, not signing a contract for a flawless future.

For a moment, picture the last event or workshop you helped organize. Now think of the student who sat at the back and said nothing. Did the design of the session help that person feel safe and included, or did all the attention go to whoever was already confident? This isn't a criticism. It's a design test. We should measure success partly by what becomes possible for the person who didn't arrive with social capital. That means asking for feedback, working within safeguarding requirements, and making sure our actions match the respectful language we use on stage.
Your future is not predetermined, and circumstances matter. But you have influence over it. Use that influence to build a life that a younger version of you would feel safe growing into.

I'll leave you with a specific assignment. Choose one part of your school or group culture you can improve within thirty days. Talk to the people affected, involve the appropriate adults or professionals, and define a realistic way to learn whether the change helped. Document the process so another group can build on it. SoberGenZ should stand for responsible action, not just confident words. Thank you for the work you do for young people.
